text: Prodigious means enormous, on a scale that startles you. It shares a root with prodigy, a young person with outsized talent, and carries the same disbelief at sheer size. Here it describes America burning through nearly two-thirds of its Patriot stockpile in one short war.

A panacea is a cure-all, one remedy that would fix every problem at once, named after the Greek goddess of universal healing. You will usually meet it in the negative: saying deep-strike weapons are no panacea concedes they help while warning they cannot end the missile threat on their own.

Proliferation is rapid multiplication and spread, the way something goes from rare to everywhere; the verb is proliferate. Here it is missile technology spreading to ever more countries and armed groups, and it is the same word inside nuclear non-proliferation, the effort to keep nuclear weapons from spreading to new states.

An interceptor is a defensive missile whose only job is to fly up and destroy an incoming missile or drone before it lands. The whole article is about the West running low on them: the best cost millions apiece and factories make only hundreds a year.

A turkey shoot is a contest so one-sided it resembles hunters firing at birds that cannot shoot back. Calling Kyiv's air war a turkey-shoot means Russian missiles increasingly arrive unopposed as Ukraine's interceptors run out.

To thwart something is to block it and make it fail. Ukraine had thwarted most missile attacks while its Patriot supplies lasted; the word usually appears exactly like this, with a plan or an attack as its victim.

Not the AAA kind. In military language a battery is a grouped set of guns or missile launchers that fire together, so a Patriot battery is the radar, control station and several launchers that make up one working unit.

Winchester is military radio code for having fired all your ammunition, borrowed from the famous rifle maker. A pilot calls Winchester when the racks are empty; the article stretches the term to a whole country running out of interceptors.

A plight is a difficult, dangerous situation someone is stuck in. Writers reach for it when the trouble is serious and not of the sufferer's choosing, like Ukraine facing missile barrages with almost nothing left to fire back.

Acute means sharp, severe, at its most intense point, the way doctors call a sudden crisis acute rather than chronic. Ukraine's shortage being the most acute sign of the West's problem means everyone shares the crisis; Ukraine feels it sharpest.

An arsenal is a country's whole store of weapons, originally the building where they were kept. America's depleted arsenal means the national stockpile itself is running down, not just one base's supply.

Depleted means used up, drained well below what you started with. It is the article's key adjective: stocks of interceptors and Tomahawks alike have been depleted faster than factories can refill them.

To divert something is to redirect it from its planned path. The Pentagon's power to divert Patriot deliveries means it can seize missiles a foreign buyer already paid for and send them wherever America needs them more, which is why no delivery date can be guaranteed.

Munitions are the things weapons actually fire: shells, rockets, bombs, missiles. Generals love buying the flashy launcher and skimp on the munitions it consumes, which is one reason the West's stockpiles are so thin.

Attritional describes a conflict won by slowly grinding the other side down, wearing away soldiers and supplies rather than landing one decisive blow. Attritional wars devour ammunition, so shortages are normal in them; America's surprise is running short after a brief war.
Here exhaust has nothing to do with tiredness or tailpipes: to exhaust a supply is to use it up completely. A war with China would exhaust America's interceptors within days.

Guam is a small American island territory in the western Pacific, home to major air and naval bases. Its location puts American forces within reach of Asia, and, increasingly, within reach of Chinese missiles.

Proximate means nearest or most immediate. The proximate cause of a crisis is the trigger that set it off just now, as opposed to the deeper causes building for years: here the Iran war is the trigger, decades of slow production the deeper cause.

The Pentagon is the five-sided building outside Washington that houses America's Department of Defense, and journalists use the name as shorthand for the American military leadership itself. When the Pentagon fires or diverts missiles, that means the defence establishment, not a building.

A think-tank is an organisation of researchers paid to study public problems and publish recommendations. This article leans on several: CSIS and Heritage in Washington, RUSI and the IISS in Britain. Their figures, like the 19,000-Patriot estimate, are expert studies, not official government numbers.

A reckoning is the moment a bill finally comes due, when consequences that built up quietly must at last be faced. The Iran war did not create the interceptor shortage; it hastened a reckoning decades in the making.

To compound a problem is to make it worse by piling more on top, the way compound interest stacks interest upon interest. The basic error of slow production was compounded by missile proliferation, budget dysfunction and complacency.

Complacency is lazy self-satisfaction: feeling so safe you stop checking whether you still are. America assumed its air power would always rule, and that complacency helped hollow out its missile defences.

Supremacy is the state of being supreme: unchallenged dominance over all rivals. American military supremacy in the air was taken for granted for so long that nobody planned for wars in which the skies are contested.
Gargantuan means gigantic, from Gargantua, a giant in an old French novel famous for his appetite. A $1.5trn defence budget, half again bigger than today's, earns the word.

A dinner jacket is British English for a tuxedo, the formal suit you might wear a handful of times in your life. That is Bronk's point in comparing the Patriot to one: you rarely need it, but on the night you do, nothing else in the wardrobe will do.
A round is one unit of ammunition, one shot's worth: a bullet is a round, and so is a $4m-5m PAC-3 interceptor. Counting weapons in rounds keeps the focus on how quickly they get used up.
Apiece simply means each, for every single one. Interceptor rounds at $4m-5m apiece means every individual missile fired costs that much.

An order of magnitude is a factor of ten, so two orders of magnitude cheaper means costing around one-hundredth as much. Scientists and engineers use the phrase to compare things of wildly different size, like a drone against the missile sent to stop it.

In military use, to field a weapon is to put it into service, to actually get it onto the battlefield in numbers. An adversary that can field cheap attack drones by the thousand poses a different problem from one that merely designs them.

Nothing to do with weddings here: in military language an engagement is a single clash between opposing forces, one interceptor against one incoming drone or missile. The colonel's warning turns on the gap between winning every engagement and winning the longer exchange of costs.

UAV stands for unmanned aerial vehicle, the military's formal term for a drone: an aircraft with no pilot aboard, flown remotely or by computer. A one-way attack UAV is built to crash into its target and explode.

Shahed is the family of cheap Iranian one-way attack drones that Russia fires at Ukrainian cities in swarms; the name means witness in Persian. Costing about as much as a used car, they exist to soak up expensive air defences.

A cruise missile is in effect a robot jet aircraft: it flies level under its own engine, often hugging the ground to stay under radar, and steers itself to the target. Slower than a ballistic missile but far more capable than a drone; today's handout compares all three.

A ballistic missile is boosted high by a rocket, often to the edge of space, then falls onto its target at several times the speed of sound. Ballistic refers to that unpowered, gravity-driven arc, like a thrown ball's. The speed of the fall is what makes these missiles so hard to intercept.

Hypersonic means flying at more than five times the speed of sound, roughly 4,000mph and up. At such speeds defenders have seconds to react, which is why hypersonic weapons are prized by attackers and dreaded by air defences.

Russia's two most feared missiles in this war. The Iskander-M is a ground-launched ballistic missile; the Kinzhal, whose name means dagger in Russian, is a version fired from high-flying jets. Only Patriot interceptors have reliably stopped either.
Dire means extremely serious, verging on hopeless, a signal that disaster is close. An interception rate that fell from 70% to 20% in four months and keeps falling is dire: a collapse, not a dip.

To solicit is to formally ask for something, especially proposals or bids. The Pentagon soliciting ideas for faster production means it has invited companies to pitch, which is much weaker than signing contracts that actually pay for it.

To make a product under licence is to build someone else's design with their permission, usually for a fee, the way a local factory might produce a global brand's shoes. Japan builds Patriot interceptors under licence, and Ukraine wants the same deal.

To upstage someone, a word borrowed from the theatre, is to steal the attention or success that was supposed to be theirs. Patriot's makers reportedly fear cheaper Ukrainian versions would upstage their own product.

Nimble means quick, light and agile, able to change direction fast. Applied to Ukraine's defence industry it praises speed of adaptation: small firms that redesign weapons in months while giant Western contractors take years.

An upstart is a newcomer that rises suddenly and challenges the established players, with a hint that the old guard finds it presumptuous. Upstart Western firms are trying to break into missile defence the way startups break into any industry.
To abound is to exist in large numbers, to be everywhere. Sceptics abound is a compact way of saying plenty of experts doubt the project will work.

A moon shot, named for the Apollo programme, is a project so ambitious it borders on unrealistic: a huge payoff if it works, long odds that it will. Calling Freyja a moon shot is a polite way of doubting that a cut-price interceptor can be built without American technology.
Wrath is fierce, vengeful anger, the kind that punishes. Risking China's wrath means inviting its retaliation, which is why few countries dare buy Taiwanese weapons.

Let alone links two things to say the second, bigger one is even less likely than the first. If the SAMP-T works less well than older Patriots, let alone newer ones, it cannot match the old models and falls even further behind the new.

The Tomahawk is America's veteran long-range cruise missile, launched from ships and submarines against targets hundreds of miles inland. A third of the 3,000-odd stockpile is already spent, showing the shortage reaches offensive weapons too.

Nothing to do with the stockmarket here: a stock is a stored supply, and military stocks are the piles of weapons a country keeps ready for war. Rebuilding Patriot stocks to pre-war levels will take until 2029.

To suppress enemy fire is to hold it down and reduce it, without necessarily ending it. America and Israel suppressed Iranian missile launches by up to 90% by bombing launchers, but suppression is not elimination: some missiles kept coming.

Exquisite usually praises delicate beauty, but applied to surveillance it means extraordinarily precise and refined, intelligence-gathering of the highest possible quality. Even with exquisite surveillance, America and Israel could not find and stop every Iranian launcher.

The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow sea passage between Iran and Arabia through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil ships. That choke-point geography is why Iranian attacks on ships there rattle the whole global economy.

Formidable describes something so powerful or difficult it inspires respect and a little fear; the word comes from the Latin for dread. A formidable enterprise is an undertaking of daunting scale, like fighting an air war across the whole Pacific.

The People's Liberation Army is the official name of China's armed forces, covering its army, navy, air force and the Rocket Force that controls its missiles. The PLA is the looming scenario behind this article: defending against it could take more than 19,000 Patriot interceptors.

In military language conventional means non-nuclear: ordinary explosives rather than atomic warheads. The danger is that China's Rocket Force controls both kinds, so a strike aimed at its conventional missiles could look like an attack on its nuclear arsenal.

Escalation is a conflict ratcheting up step by step, each side answering with something bigger until events pass anyone's control. Nuclear escalation is the ultimate version, and avoiding even a first step toward it shapes every American war plan involving China.

Dispersal is deliberately spreading things out so that one strike cannot destroy them all: parking aircraft at many small airfields instead of one big base. It is the survival strategy for operating inside the reach of Chinese missiles.

In defence-speak, hardening means physically toughening a target against attack: thicker concrete, buried bunkers, blast doors. A hardened target forces the enemy to spend more and bigger missiles to destroy it.

To deter an attack is to prevent it by making the attacker expect unbearable costs, so the strike never happens at all. As the general says, the cheapest interceptor is the one you never fire; weapons that deter earn their keep without ever launching.

To scramble is to rush frantically, all elbows and improvisation. Allies scrambling for deep-strike weapons are hurrying to buy or build them in the slightly panicked way of people who have realised they are late.

To take heed is to pay serious attention to a warning and act on it, an old-fashioned phrase that makes a sentence sound like advice carved in stone. The article's closing line tells other governments to learn from Ukraine's plight before it becomes their own.
A hitch is a snag, the catch that complicates an otherwise fine plan. The hitch with interceptors is arithmetic: each one costs more than the missile it is trying to destroy.

Reckon here is the British usage meaning estimates or concludes after doing the sums, not the cowboy's casual I reckon. When CSIS reckons rebuilding will take until 2029, that is a think-tank's calculated judgment.
